covers.quote: Place a comma after adverbs and other introductory words
You don’t need a comma after an introductory word if the sentence is very short. This minimises punctuation in very short sentences.

parts.quote: Yes, they went to the estimates hearing. [Affirmative emphasis]
Goodnight, and good luck. [Greeting]
Actually, that's an interesting point. [Adverb]
Excuse me, should I come with you? [Addressing someone]

examples.note: Example of a very short sentence omitting the comma

parts.quote: Today I went to work.

rules.quote: Use a comma after introductory words, such as greetings and adverbs, or when addressing someone.
rules.specification: Threshold for 'very short' sentence must be chosen (e.g., 4 words or fewer) to apply the exception.
rules.violation_condition: an introductory word (like a greeting, adverb, or address) at the start of a sentence that is not followed by a comma
when: You don’t need a comma after an introductory word if the sentence is very short.
rules.why: G-2: The exception for short sentences modifies when the rule applies. G-4: Quoted the body sentence rather than the heading.

covers.quote: Use a comma after phrases and clauses that change the whole sentence
Conditional clauses are adverbial clauses (for example, beginning with ‘if’, ‘unless’ or ‘until’). They should also have a comma after them if they start the sentence.

parts.quote: During the meeting, we discussed item 9. [Adverbial phrase]
Although they were shaking and sweating, the firefighters were relieved to feel the first drops of a downpour. [Adverbial clause]
Unless the consultation starts early, it will not finish on time. [A conditional adverbial clause]

rules.quote: Use commas after adverbial phrases and adverbial clauses.
rules.violation_condition: an adverbial or conditional phrase/clause starting a sentence without a comma following it
when: Conditional clauses should have a comma after them if they start the sentence.
rules.why: G-4: Rule restated in heading, quoted the more specific body instruction. G-2: Conditional clauses are a specific sub-case of adverbial clauses.

covers.quote: Use a comma after an introductory phrase that ends with a numeral and is immediately followed by another numeral. It doesn’t matter how short the sentence is.
Avoid this type of sentence structure because the string of numbers can be confusing.

parts.quote: There were 16.5 million people enrolled to vote in Australian elections on 18 April 2019.
On 18 April 2019, 16.5 million people were enrolled to vote in Australian elections.

rules.quote: Avoid beginning a sentence with a string of numbers and dates
rules.violation_condition: a sentence beginning with a string of numbers and dates adjacent to each other
when: If you must, use a comma after an introductory phrase that ends with a numeral and is immediately followed by another numeral.
rules.why: G-2: Avoidance of structure and fallback punctuation rule grouped as they address the same violating text.

covers.quote: Set off non-essential clauses
Don’t use commas if the clause is essential for meaning.
If you can remove the clause and your sentence means the same thing, it’s non-essential and should go between commas.
Non-essential clauses are also called ‘non-restrictive’ or ‘non-defining’ clauses.

parts.quote: The business report, which the manager had edited, explained the agency’s strategy.
Introduced pests, such as varroa mite, threaten Australian honey production.
The report that the manager had edited explained the agency’s strategy.
Introduced pests from South Asia threaten Australian honey production.

rules.quote: Use commas around clauses that add information but aren’t essential to the meaning of the sentence.
rules.violation_condition: a non-essential (non-restrictive) clause that is not enclosed in a pair of commas
when: Don’t use commas if the clause is essential for meaning.
rules.why: G-4: Used body sentence instead of heading. G-2: Exclusions for essential meaning grouped.

covers.quote: Check if you can rephrase the information to make it easier to follow. It is easier for people to read shorter sentences.

parts.quote: The report was tabled last week. It is about demographic changes in rural areas in Western Australia.
The report, detailing demographic changes in rural areas in Western Australia, was tabled last week.

rules.quote: Each of these examples separates a grammatical subject from its verb. This is a problem when the subject is overburdened with non-essential information.
rules.specification: Requires defining a length or complexity threshold for 'overburdened' to automate.
rules.violation_condition: a grammatical subject separated from its verb by an excessively long or complex non-essential clause
rules.why: Derived from the manual's Write this/Not this example highlighting overburdened subjects as errors.

covers.quote: Place commas around nouns that define the same thing they follow
You should be able to take out the noun phrase between the comma pair and still have a grammatically correct sentence.

parts.quote: The strike took place in Whyalla, South Australia, in June 2014.
The strike took place in Whyalla, South Australia in June 2014.
My colleague, Mx Lesley May, will exercise my proxy vote.
My colleague will exercise my proxy vote.

rules.quote: Use a pair of commas when you have 2 noun phrases next to each other that define the same thing.
rules.violation_condition: two adjacent noun phrases defining the same thing (appositives) not separated by a pair of commas
rules.why: G-4: Rule restated in heading, body sentence quoted. E-1: Examples marked correct.

covers.quote: Separate questions tagged onto a sentence

parts.quote: They’re not here, are they?
We’ll be reporting back, won’t we?

rules.quote: Use a comma before a question that is part of the sentence.
rules.violation_condition: a question tag appended to the end of a sentence not preceded by a comma
rules.why: G-4: Quote body instruction over heading.

covers.quote: Use commas with the phrase ‘for example’
If ‘for example’ begins a sentence, it is an introductory phrase. Follow it with a comma.
If you’re introducing a bullet list after ‘for example’, use a colon.

parts.quote: Some colours, for example, are difficult for people with colour blindness to distinguish.
For example, some colours are difficult for people with colour blindness to distinguish.

examples.note: E-3: The list lead-in and its items represent one complete example.

parts.quote: Some colours are difficult for people with colour blindness to distinguish, for example:
red
green
orange
brown
blue
purple.

rules.quote: Generally, use a comma before and after the phrase ‘for example’ in a sentence.
rules.violation_condition: the phrase 'for example' occurring inline without commas around it, at the start of a sentence without a trailing comma, or introducing a bullet list without a trailing colon
when: If ‘for example’ begins a sentence, follow it with a comma.
If you’re introducing a bullet list after ‘for example’, use a colon.
rules.why: G-2: The different punctuations depend on location/role (inline, start, or introducing a list) but are triggered by the exact phrase.

covers.quote: Don’t use commas with Latin shortened forms

parts.quote: Exports of rare earths (e.g. lithium, europium) have soared.
Exports of rare earths (e.g., lithium and europium) have soared.

rules.quote: If you use Latin shortened forms, such as ‘e.g.’ and ‘i.e.’, don’t follow them with a comma.
rules.violation_condition: a Latin shortened form (like 'e.g.' or 'i.e.') followed by a comma
rules.why: G-4: Quote the body instruction.

covers.quote: Place commas between principal clauses joined together with a conjunction
If they have different subjects, use a comma before the coordinating conjunction.
If 2 clauses share the same subject, you don’t need to repeat the subject or insert a comma before the conjunction.
The exception to this rule is when you have joined more than 2 principal clauses with the same subject.

parts.quote: The Senate debated the Bill at length, but the party whips eventually called for a vote.
The company closed its Perth office and sacked the chief financial officer.
The company closed its Perth office, sacked the chief financial officer, and opened a branch in Singapore.

rules.quote: Use commas to connect 2 or more principal clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (‘and’, ‘or’, ‘but’, ‘so’).
rules.violation_condition: two or more principal clauses with different subjects joined by a coordinating conjunction without a preceding comma, or more than two principal clauses with the same subject joined without commas
when: If they have different subjects, use a comma before the coordinating conjunction.
If 2 clauses share the same subject, you don't need to repeat the subject or insert a comma before the conjunction.
Use commas if you have joined more than 2 principal clauses with the same subject.
rules.why: G-2: The exact example from the policy text regarding clauses sharing subjects versus differing ones triggering the same check.

rules.quote: Do not use this rule to create a sentence of more than 25 words.
rules.violation_condition: a sentence exceeding 25 words created by joining principal clauses with coordinating conjunctions
rules.why: A discrete constraint on sentence length attached to the rule for joining clauses.

covers.quote: Don’t use commas to ‘splice’ sentences

parts.quote: The report was finished last week, but the minister has not approved its release.
The report was finished last week, the minister has not approved its release.

rules.quote: Don’t use a comma to link 2 stand-alone sentences unless you use a coordinating conjunction.
rules.violation_condition: two independent clauses joined only by a comma (comma splice)
rules.why: G-4: Quote the body instruction over the heading.

covers.quote: Separate items in lists of nouns or adjectives with commas
This rule applies to sentence lists and sentence fragments in bullet lists. Do not punctuate the end of a list item with a comma if it is in a bullet list.

parts.quote: The delegation visited Brisbane, Canberra and Adelaide.
The consultation involved businesses, sole traders and not-for-profits.
The applicant was willing to learn, eager to work and well prepared.

rules.quote: Use commas between items in a sentence list. Avoid using a comma before the last item in the list.
rules.violation_condition: items in a sentence list not separated by commas, or a comma placed before the final item in a simple list
when: Do not punctuate the end of a list item with a comma if it is in a bullet list.
rules.why: G-4: Quote the main sentence.

covers.quote: Restrict the use of the Oxford comma
The Oxford comma can prevent ambiguity in complex sentence lists. For example, use the Oxford comma before the last item if you’re using a defining phrase applicable only to that final item.
A defining phrase is essential to the meaning of the sentence. The following examples show how the Oxford comma can affect meaning, using the defining phrase ‘for stockfeed’.

parts.quote: The industries most affected are retail trade, wholesale trade, and accommodation and food services.

examples.note: E-1: Contrast pair shown as compliant because it represents correct usage reflecting a different meaning.

parts.quote: The analysis outlined demand for barley, wheat and hay for stockfeed. [All crops are for stockfeed.]

examples.note: E-1: Contrast pair showing how Oxford comma changes meaning correctly.

parts.quote: The analysis outlined demand for barley, wheat, and hay for stockfeed. [Only the hay is for stockfeed.]

rules.quote: If the last item combines 2 words or phrases with the word ‘and’, use a comma before that final item.
rules.violation_condition: a list where the last item contains 'and' internally, but is not preceded by an Oxford comma; or where the last item has a defining phrase but lacks an Oxford comma
when: Use the Oxford comma before the last item if you’re using a defining phrase applicable only to that final item.
rules.why: G-2: The specific triggers that mandate an Oxford comma are grouped together.

rules.quote: When writing strings of adjectives, use a set order – evaluative, descriptive, then definitive.
rules.violation_condition: a string of adjectives that does not follow the set order: evaluative, descriptive, definitive
rules.why: Distinct rule regarding the grammatical order of adjectives, independent of how they are punctuated.

covers.quote: Separate adjectives of the same type
Don’t use commas in strings of adjectives of different types.

parts.quote: This is an ethical, profitable, efficient organisation. [Descriptive adjectives]
They were a happy, caring, devoted workforce. [Evaluative adjectives]
My new black felt-tip pen splattered ink everywhere.
We found some used French tennis balls left over from a training day.

rules.quote: Use commas in strings of adjectives of the same type (for example, a string of descriptive adjectives).
rules.violation_condition: a string of adjectives of the same type not separated by commas, or adjectives of different types separated by commas
when: Don’t use commas in strings of adjectives of different types.
rules.why: G-2: The comma requirement changes based on adjective types being identical or mixed.

covers.quote: Use commas in numbers with 4 or more digits
Don’t use a space between the digits, because screen readers can read them as separate numbers.
When you are using numbers of 1,000 or more, use commas to separate the numerals into groups of 3 (working right to left).
Commas are not used to the right of a decimal point.
Don’t use commas in postcodes or dates.

parts.quote: The agency handles around 6,500 complaints each year.
The agency handles around 6 500 complaints each year. [This can be read as the number 6 followed by the number 500.]
The year was 2020.
The office was in postcode area 6500.

rules.quote: Numbers with 4 or more digits (starting from 1,000) need a comma.
rules.violation_condition: a number of 4 or more digits written without a thousands comma, other than a year or postcode or the digits after a decimal point, or written with a space instead of a comma
when: Use commas for numerals in text and in tables.
Use commas to separate the numerals into groups of 3 (working right to left).
Don't use a space between the digits.
Commas are not used to the right of a decimal point.
Don’t use commas in postcodes or dates.
rules.why: G-2: Number comma punctuation triggers and exclusions combined into one rule.

covers.quote: Show direct speech or quoted material using commas
If an attribution comes after a quotation, use a comma at the end of the quotation and before the quotation mark.
If the quotation is broken into 2 parts, the second part should follow a full stop rather than a comma.
If the quotation ends the sentence, end it with the original punctuation of the quotation.

parts.quote: She said, ‘It’s time to start work.’
The Prime Minister said, ‘I’m calling a half-Senate election.’
‘It’s time to start work,’ she said.
‘I’m calling a half-Senate election for Saturday 15 August,’ the Prime Minister said.
‘It’s time to start work,’ she said. ‘We have a lot to do.’
‘I’m calling a half-Senate election,’ the Prime Minister said. ‘It will be held on Saturday 15 August.’
She said, ‘It’s time to start work.’
She asked, ‘Is it time to start work?’

rules.quote: Introduce directly quoted speech with a comma.

when: Use the comma in combination with quotation marks.

A defining phrase is essential to the meaning of the sentence. The following examples show how the Oxford comma can affect meaning, using the defining phrase ‘for stockfeed’.

parts.quote: The industries most affected are retail trade, wholesale trade, and accommodation and food services.

examples.note: E-1: Contrast pair shown as compliant because it represents correct usage reflecting a different meaning.

parts.quote: The analysis outlined demand for barley, wheat and hay for stockfeed. [All crops are for stockfeed.]

examples.note: E-1: Contrast pair showing how Oxford comma changes meaning correctly.

parts.quote: The analysis outlined demand for barley, wheat, and hay for stockfeed. [Only the hay is for stockfeed.]

tags.violation_condition: a list where the last item contains 'and' internally, but is not preceded by an Oxford comma; or where the last item has a defining phrase but lacks an Oxford comma

when: Use the Oxford comma before the last item if you’re using a defining phrase applicable only to that final item.
rules.why: G-2: The specific triggers that mandate an Oxford comma are grouped together.

anchor.quote: When writing strings of adjectives, use a set order – evaluative, descriptive, then definitive.

tags.violation_condition: a string of adjectives that does not follow the set order: evaluative, descriptive, definitive

rules.why: Distinct rule regarding the grammatical order of adjectives, independent of how they are punctuated.

anchor.quote: Use commas in strings of adjectives of the same type (for example, a string of descriptive adjectives).

covers.quote: Separate adjectives of the same type
Don’t use commas in strings of adjectives of different types.

parts.quote: This is an ethical, profitable, efficient organisation. [Descriptive adjectives]
They were a happy, caring, devoted workforce. [Evaluative adjectives]
My new black felt-tip pen splattered ink everywhere.
We found some used French tennis balls left over from a training day.

tags.violation_condition: a string of adjectives of the same type not separated by commas, or adjectives of different types separated by commas

when: Don’t use commas in strings of adjectives of different types.
rules.why: G-2: The comma requirement changes based on adjective types being identical or mixed.

anchor.quote: Numbers with 4 or more digits (starting from 1,000) need a comma.
anchor.suffix: Use commas for numerals in text

covers.quote: Use commas in numbers with 4 or more digits
Don’t use a space between the digits, because screen readers can read them as separate numbers.
When you are using numbers of 1,000 or more, use commas to separate the numerals into groups of 3 (working right to left).
Commas are not used to the right of a decimal point.
Don’t use commas in postcodes or dates.

parts.quote: The agency handles around 6,500 complaints each year.
The agency handles around 6 500 complaints each year. [This can be read as the number 6 followed by the number 500.]
The year was 2020.
The office was in postcode area 6500.

tags.violation_condition: a number of 4 or more digits written without a thousands comma, other than a year or postcode or the digits after a decimal point, or written with a space instead of a comma

when: Use commas for numerals in text and in tables.
Use commas to separate the numerals into groups of 3 (working right to left).
Don't use a space between the digits.
Commas are not used to the right of a decimal point.
Don’t use commas in postcodes or dates.
rules.why: G-2: Number comma punctuation triggers and exclusions combined into one rule.

anchor.quote: Introduce directly quoted speech with a comma.
anchor.suffix: Use the comma in combination wi

covers.quote: Show direct speech or quoted material using commas
If an attribution comes after a quotation, use a comma at the end of the quotation and before the quotation mark.
If the quotation is broken into 2 parts, the second part should follow a full stop rather than a comma.
If the quotation ends the sentence, end it with the original punctuation of the quotation.

parts.quote: She said, ‘It’s time to start work.’
The Prime Minister said, ‘I’m calling a half-Senate election.’
‘It’s time to start work,’ she said.
‘I’m calling a half-Senate election for Saturday 15 August,’ the Prime Minister said.
‘It’s time to start work,’ she said. ‘We have a lot to do.’
‘I’m calling a half-Senate election,’ the Prime Minister said. ‘It will be held on Saturday 15 August.’
She said, ‘It’s time to start work.’
She asked, ‘Is it time to start work?’

tags.violation_condition: directly quoted speech not introduced by a comma, or incorrectly punctuated when attributions follow or break the quote

when: Use the comma in combination with quotation marks.
If an attribution comes after a quotation, use a comma at the end of the quotation and before the quotation mark.
If the quotation is broken into 2 parts, the second part should follow a full stop rather than a comma.
If the quotation ends the sentence, end it with the original punctuation of the quotation.
rules.why: G-2: The specific variations for punctuating quotations are based on where attributions appear, but involve checking the same punctuation structure.
